title: A Wet Time in the Woods with Dillen and Emerson: Bikepacking from Bellingham to Whistler – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
Dillen Wilder lost his foot in a cycling accident, but not his love of the ride. Since moving to Bellingham, Washington, he’s found recovery, friendship, and a new perspective in the Heavy Bike Club, a judgment-free crew that favors the bikes they love over the newest, lightest gear. Dillen shares how that mindset led him and his friend Emerson to load up their steel hardtails and ride nearly 200 miles through relentless Pacific Northwest rain, all to get to the Whistler Bike Park. It’s a story about sustainability, community, and the idea that the ride to the trailhead might be the best part of all.

The Heavy Bike Club

After losing my foot in a cycling accident, I moved in with my family to be closer to the kind of medical care and support I’d need as I learned to navigate life as an amputee. The community I found in this new city has been vital to my recovery; as essential as any doctor. While I developed a new relationship with bikes, I gravitated toward a cycling niche that might seem counterintuitive for a fella with mobility challenges: the Heavy Bike Club. Defined by folks who choose what they have and love over shiny new lightweight gear, the Heavy Bike Club is an intentionally judgement-free space for people to show up as they are and ride any distance. I found folks who did not seem to mind if I needed to take a break. No one rolled their eyes if I slowed down the group. My new friends are excited to be out on bikes and connecting with their local environment.

We are lucky here in Bellingham to have Kim and Andrew, owners of the local bike/coffee shop Cafe Velo. They are the humble unofficial figureheads of our Heavy Bike Club. It’s a motley group of individuals who certainly don’t mind riding a little slower to soak up extra moments on long summer days. They ride their own heavy bikes, and always encourage me when I’m dreaming up some new alterations to my own steel creations. Oh yeah, I build my own bikes.

Confused Looks

At first glance, the cycling community in Bellingham appears dominated by mountain bikers. Some, like me, would fall into the Heavy Bike Club with their older frames and (by industry standards) outdated components. Many would say they have other priorities. You may know the type: those with the newest carbon enduro bikes who drive their truck to the trailhead and rip hot laps with the boys. They cap their ride with a little “Vitamin R” (that’s Rainier beer for the uninitiated) in the parking lot. Some of these folks would never consider commuting by bike, or even riding a bike in a situation that doesn’t require knee pads. Not throwing shade, just describing the best-catered-to demographic in the Bellingham cycling industry. I love a “send train” down the jump line as much as the next mountain biker. However, I also adore steel hardtails. The bikes that are far more focused on the feel of the ride rather than the top speed of the ride. The bikes that draw confused looks from many at my local trailhead.

Steel is Sustainable

One of the biggest draws toward a steel hardtail for me is sustainability. A steel bicycle frame can outlive its original owner. When humanity comes to an end, a steel bicycle frame will slowly oxidize into dust and provide important nutrients for whatever critters that live on after our demise. That might be an odd thing to think about when choosing one’s preferred method of recreation, but these are things I think about.

I have been lucky to spend time in many corners of the cycling industry; from mass production to niche bespoke fabrication. One thing that stuck with me from my time working in factories was the volume of waste. Bicycles are routinely touted as green transportation, and an excellent way to stay fit while helping our ailing ecosystem. Yet here I was throwing away single-use foam bags used to protect high-end carbon components for assembly into high-end carbon bicycles. That was hard to justify in my mind. What about the future critters after the death of society? Where would they get their iron oxide if everyone is riding bikes made with synthetic epoxies that won’t gracefully degrade and feed the ecosystem?

Though in all seriousness, when I learned of wireless shifters built to be tossed once the battery dies, my head started spinning. Who asked for that? Products made and sold just because they can be. I feel like Dr. Ian Malcom in Jurassic Park saying, “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.” Do I have a solution for the continuous push towards new and “better” just because we can? No. I don’t think I can stop consumerism any more than I can stop asteroids from colliding with our planet. However, I do think it’s essential for cyclists, wherever they sit on the spectrum, to ask ourselves why we like to ride.

How does it improve cycling to build bigger parking lots at local trailheads? As an adaptive athlete, I love seeing accessible parking spaces at trailheads. I applaud making trails accessible for electric mountain bikes to get more folks out there on trails I love dearly. Riding IS for everyone, after all. Finding community in the cycling world is a wonderful experience that I want everyone to have. However, at what point is “more” actually improving the experiences we have on bikes?

An Ugly Flower

Pondering these questions planted a weird seed in my head. On the first weekend of June, this seed grew into a misshapen, foul-smelling, yet glorious flower.

Mountain biking was my first love. I’ve had more than one friend insinuate I am in an abusive relationship with mountain biking considering how much physical and emotional strife it has put me through. Yet I always come crawling back for more. When I discovered the joys of bikepacking, my relationship with mountain biking found more depth and beauty. In fact, I proselytize bikepacking a little too much to anyone who will stick around long enough to listen.

So one day, while at work in one of Bellingham’s many bike shops, that little seed in my head sprouted when I told my co-worker, “Wouldn’t it be cool to ride from here to Whistler Bike Park and do a few laps?” The ultimate “let’s just ride to the trailhead” experience.

Just Ride to the Trailhead

I love riding my mountain bike to our local trailheads here in Bellingham. But to a bike park? That was a crazy thought. To my delight, my co-worker gave an emphatic “YES.” This co-worker, Emerson, used to race downhill competitively and is a talented bike mechanic. This amazing lad undoubtedly knows his way around a bike. Last year, we designed and built him a rowdy custom hardtail that he’s been ripping around on for months now. He has thus slowly dipped his toes into the Heavy Bike Club. Seems he likes the vibes. So, we started scheming.

We would ride our steel hardtails, with everything we would need strapped to them, from my house in Bellingham to the Whistler Bike Park. All the while hitting as much singletrack along the way as we had the energy for. Just ride to the trailhead.

Our route changed many times after that first conversation. Out-of-date intel and overzealous bites of challenging singletrack eventually led us to the final route. Poor Emerson had never ridden more than 70-ish miles on any bike ever, let alone a loaded mountain bike. Yet he performed admirably. He embraced his newfound Heavy Bike Club label and helped me through this wild adventure. Even though I’ve put in more miles bikepacking, he’s much faster. Every time he came back to help me lift my heavy bike over a steep rooted section of singletrack, it filled me with joy to be out there with my friend. I’m so happy that we did this crazy thing together. Every step of the way, we made decisions together and embraced the bonkers conditions we got ourselves into. That is what it feels like to be accepted and embraced in your community. Working together towards a common goal is a beautiful thing, even if that goal is pretty absurd.

Bikepacking from Bellingham to Whistler

It took us three days to ride from Bellingham to Whistler, and it was the worst weather window in months. When we weren’t actively being rained on, we were chasing ominous grey skies. We had originally planned on cowboy camping. Mother Nature had other plans. With the added weight of our full tents, we rode off into the rain on a Sunday morning, lacing together dozens of miles of Bellingham’s greenways as we went deeper into Whatcom County. Quickly we found ourselves on an overgrown singletrack through the woods. This early assault by blackberry thorns set the scene for our shenanigans to come.

We rode and hiked our bikes for days through overgrown, washed-out, and muddy trails or roads with one unexpected detour after another. We rode at least one blue-rated singletrack per day while on our way up to the bike park (Noodley Appendage, CRC, and Man Boobs, for those curious). I could talk about the laughter and heartbreak for hours. The biggest takeaway? I had a blast mountain biking with my friend. I got to share my love of bikepacking with him. Stopping to look at cool trees and huge banana slugs while snacking on weird foods that just so happened to have the right form factor to fit in our bags. All the while smelling like a wet dog that may have rolled in something dead while you weren’t looking. (We never did dry out with the amount of rain we encountered; it was a truly Pacific Northwest experience.) Then, when we reached our destination, Emerson got to share with me some of his favorite lift-access trails. A melding of worlds. We embraced each other’s style of cycling and found a way to combine them.

To top it off, after almost 200 miles and over 20,000 feet of elevation gain got us just south of Whistler Village, we hitched the final few miles. A kind fellow dirtbag named Martin offered us a lift in the pouring rain. Those last few miles in Martin’s beat-up old pickup were glorious. He dropped us in the village and said he hoped we enjoyed our laps at the bike park. Thanks, Martin!

We rode our bikes to the trailhead (mostly). What is usually a three-hour drive, we turned into three days of moist mountain biking on quirky steel bikes. All of that for three amazing laps of the Whistler Bike Park. Did we reroute the onslaught of consumerism away from destroying our beloved natural spaces? Absolutely not. Did we offset our waste in a reasonable way? Almost certainly not. However, we did blow quite a few minds along the way. Every trail user who stopped to chat was amazed at the journey. Just a simple ride to the trailhead.

Do It Yourself

So, please, give it a try. Let your mind visit those strange recesses when thinking about the ecological impact of your choices. Or, if you don’t want to burden yourselves with the fate of the natural world, just go have fun on a ride with some cool people. Build community. Next time you are going for a mountain bike ride, give thought as to how you could make the ride to your favorite trails more memorable. Invite a friend. Maybe stop at the local taqueria, or maybe you will discover a new urban trail on the way there. This beautiful world is full of surprises. Some of them are delightful, and some of them are devastating. Seeing what is around the next corner is exciting regardless. Whatever is around that corner, though, we are in it together. I am going to keep riding to the trailhead every chance I get. I guess they were onto something when they said the journey is more important than the destination. Hope to see you out there!
